platforms.title: It's Not Cleaning — Cotton Swabs Push Earwax Deeper
platforms.meta_description: A survey found 31.9% of cotton swab users report ear complications. Swabs pack earwax deeper toward the eardrum instead of removing it, worsening the blockage.
platforms.body_html:
Reaching for a cotton swab to clear a muffled, plugged-up ear feels productive — but in most cases it does the opposite, packing wax deeper toward the eardrum instead of removing it.

A study surveying cotton swab users, published in the medical literature, found that 31.9% reported a complication from the habit, breaking down to roughly 21.4% reporting ear discomfort, 10.5% reporting cerumen (earwax) impaction, and 9.2% reporting some degree of hearing loss. Earwax is designed to work its way out on its own, pushed along the ear canal by everyday jaw movement from talking and chewing; the less it's interfered with, the better that natural system tends to work.

Three habits explain why some people end up with plugged, muffled ears more than others. The first is digging with cotton swabs, which — as above — tends to compact wax rather than clear it. The second is wearing earphones or hearing aids for long stretches: a blocked ear canal traps humidity and makes it physically harder for wax to migrate outward, so it clumps instead. The third is simply ignoring the muffled feeling for too long — the longer wax sits undisturbed, the more it hardens, and hardened wax is much harder for the ear to clear on its own than soft, fresh wax.

Stop Digging — Start Doing This Instead

  • Wipe only what's visible at the entrance of the ear with a soft tissue or towel — most earwax clears itself this far without any help, so there's no need to reach further in.
  • Take earphones out periodically to let the ear canal air out, and clean hearing aids on the schedule in their manual — moisture buildup is what turns loose wax into clumps.
  • Use an over-the-counter cerumenolytic (earwax softener) for a few days if wax has already hardened, rather than using it continuously — short-term use is safer than relying on it as a daily habit, and it gives the ear canal a chance to reset before wax builds up again.

How Common This Really Is

Impacted earwax is far from rare. Research on the condition estimates that it affects around 5 percent of healthy adults, but the rate climbs sharply with age and reduced mobility — up to 57 percent of elderly residents in nursing homes deal with impacted earwax, largely because reduced jaw movement and more frequent hearing aid use both slow down the ear's natural clearing process. That's not a sign of poor hygiene; it's the same mechanical system described above, just working against more obstacles.

If the muffled feeling doesn't clear up on its own, or comes with pain, drainage, or fever, it's worth having a doctor remove the impacted wax safely with proper irrigation tools rather than continuing to try to dig it out at home, which usually only makes the underlying blockage worse over time and delays the moment your ear finally clears on its own, sometimes for weeks longer than it really needed to in the first place.
